newsitem.title: USA: Wheat prices tumble as buyers shun U.S. grain.
newsitem.headline: Wheat prices tumble as buyers shun U.S. grain.

text.p: Wheat futures prices tumbled at three major U.S. futures exchanges Wednesday partly in reaction to foreign buyers shunning U.S. wheat in favour of Australian and Argentinian grain.

Crude oil prices edged higher, shrugging off U.N. action that may soon allow Iraq oil on the world market. Copper prices closed higher for the third consecutive day as low stockpiles continue to drive buying.
Major U.S. commodity futures markets will be closed Thursday in observance of the Thanksgiving Day holiday.

Wheat prices sped lower in light pre-holiday trading in Chicago, Kansas City and Minneapolis futures markets after Sri Lanka passed up U.S. wheat and bought 50,000 metric tons each of Australian and Argentinian wheat Wednesday.
Also, Morocco announced it will buy 20,000 metric tons of Argentinian wheat this week.

Traders said recent incidences of disease in U.S. wheat plus higher prices have hurt exports. As a result, wheat normally destined for export may be delivered against futures contracts, which they said is a bearish situtation.

"We continue to receive press reports about the disease problems we've had and we don't hear about that in the Argentine and Australian crops," said Joe Victor, vice president of research at the grain research firm Allendale Inc., in Crystal Lake, Ill.
Fungal diseases such as TCK and karnal bunt have been found in the U.S. wheat.

Although the wheat export pace has slowed, analysts and traders said robust sales early this year has the United States on track to meet U.S. Agriculture Department projections of 950 million bushels.

Selling intensified in wheat futures markets late Wednesday as rumours circulated that one million to two million bushels may be posted Friday against CBOT wheat contracts. Large deliveries are considered bearish because it indicates weak demand by flour millers and exporters.

Chicago Board of Trade December soft red winter wheat closed down 12-1/2 cents at $4.00-1/2 per bushel. Kansas City Board of Trade hard red winter wheat closed down six cents at $4.44 and Minneapolis Grain Exchange December spring wheat was down 2-3/4 at $4.20-1/2.
New York Mercantile Exchange crude oil futures closed higher on shortcovering ahead of the holiday.

Crude oil traders said they expected United Nations approval of an oil export pricing formula for Iraq. Other lesser hurdles must be cleared before Iraq can sell export oil for the first time in six years. An Iraqi official said "Iraqi oil will be on the market by the year end."
Crude for January delivery closed up 13 cents at $23.75 per barrel. NYMEX gasoline for January delivery rose 34 cents cent to 69.35 cents per gallon.
COMEX copper ended higher on shortcovering ahead of the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday and ahead of a closely watched London Metal Exchange stock report due Friday.
"There was some shortcovering as the holiday period is a long one, but beyond that supplies are tight," said Bette Raptopoulos of Prudential Securities.
Spot December settled 2.10 cents higher at 110.30 cents a lb, largely reflecting six-year low LME inventories.
